name: Name-letter effect
statement: People rate the letters in their own name, above all their initials, as more attractive than other letters.
meaning: Nuttin's claim is narrow. Shown the alphabet and asked which letters they like, people put the letters of their own name near the top, and their initials highest of all. A second claim was attached later, and it is the one that made the finding useful to other researchers. If people like their initials because they like themselves, then rating the alphabet is a back door to self-esteem that a respondent cannot manage. That instrument is the Name Letter Test, also called the Initial Preference Task, and it became one of the two standard measures of implicit self-esteem alongside the Implicit Association Test. The two claims stand or fall separately. Pelham's extension of the same premise to careers, towns and spouses is a third claim, treated under nominative determinism.

origin.note: The paper is titled "Narcissism beyond Gestalt and awareness: The name letter effect". Its abstract tests "mere belongingness to self" as a sufficient condition for the enhancement of the attractiveness of visual letter stimuli, and reports the preference as holding independent of visual, acoustical, aesthetic, semantic and frequency characteristics. Nuttin followed it in 1987 with a study across twelve European languages. Neither paper is about self-esteem: his term is mere ownership. Buhrmester, Blanton and Swann trace the reading of letter preference as a carryover from high self-esteem to Greenwald and Banaji in 1995.

evidence: Nuttin's first design was yoked, which holds letter frequency constant. Thirty-eight primary school girls picked the more attractive letter from each of a series of pairs. Every list was judged twice, once by the owner of the name hidden in it and once by a partner who did not own that name. Owners chose the hidden name's letters on 55.1% of pairs against 44.6% for their partners. A second study on 96 university students got the same result through rejections rather than choices, 53.8% against 37.3% non-rejection. The 1987 study dropped the yoking and asked students from twelve European countries to pick their six favourite letters from the whole alphabet. A letter reached that set 30% of the time when it belonged to the rater's name and 20% when it did not, rising to 46% for own initials, with a reliable effect in nine of the twelve groups. Those figures are read from Vera Hoorens's 1990 review, which sets both papers out in detail; the papers themselves sit behind a paywall these checks did not pass. Bosson, Swann and Pennebaker measured the same preference in American undergraduates and found initials rated 0.93 scale points above what those same letters scored from people who did not own them, t = 6.13.

replication.headline: The letter preference holds in large and varied samples; its reading as a measure of self-esteem does not.
replication.detail: Stieger and LeBel gave a letter-rating task to 1,380 people of mixed age. They report reliable preferences for the initials of a new married surname and for the initials of an abandoned birth name, still there after twenty years of marriage. The effect appeared in every age cohort tested. That paper was read here at its abstract. Bosson, Swann and Pennebaker's initials task produced a positivity bias of 0.93 scale points, t = 6.13, in 84 undergraduates. What fails is the step to self-esteem. Pietschnig and thirteen co-authors meta-analysed 60 studies covering 105 independent adult samples and 17,777 people. They put the correlation between the Initial Preference Task and explicit self-esteem at r = .102, 95% CI .079 to .125, about 1% of shared variance. They report internal consistencies from the low .30s to the low .50s and retest reliabilities from the high .30s to the high .60s, and end by saying that the latent construct measured by the task remains unclear. Bosson's single sample showed the same shape: the initials task correlated .13, .11, .09 and .13 with four explicit self-esteem measures, none of them reliable, and -.06 with the self-esteem Implicit Association Test. Its retest correlation over a mean of 31.23 days was .63, the second best of seven implicit measures and below the Rosenberg scale's .80. Buhrmester, Blanton and Swann reviewed 40 name-letter studies against 79 Implicit Association Test studies and concluded that the name-letter test is best understood as a measure of implicit egotism rather than of self-esteem.

study.cite: Stieger, S., & LeBel, E. P. (2012). Name-letter preferences for new last name and abandoned birth name initials in the context of name-change via marriage. Social Psychology, 43(1), 7-13.

limits: The numbers depend on how they are computed. Pietschnig's group report an average Cronbach's alpha of .47 for the I-algorithm and .48 for the S-algorithm. The implicit-explicit correlation itself moved with the scoring rule, .13 for the B-algorithm against .06 for the others. It also came to .11 for a single administration against .02 for a double one. Stieger, Voracek and Formann had already given the question of how to run the task two meta-analyses, k = 49 and N = 11,514, plus an experiment on 449 people. Reliability is not the only problem. Hoorens reports that in a control study by Nuttin not one participant identified the own-letter pattern in the materials, even when offered money for it, but the modern task puts the initials in plain view. Krizan found that close to half of respondents recognise what the task is for and that those who do score higher on it, which is read here from Buhrmester's account of his paper rather than from the paper. Whether initial and non-initial preferences measure one thing is also open. Hoorens and colleagues followed 164 community participants daily for a week and again at six months. They report initial preferences moving with state self-esteem while non-initial preferences tracked trait self-esteem. That paper was read at its abstract. Two further items could not be obtained. Hoorens's 2014 review in the European Review of Social Psychology is paywalled, as are Krizan's 2008 paper and Krizan and Suls's meta-analysis, whose name-letter to Rosenberg correlation of .12 across 19 estimates is quoted here from Buhrmester's table.
misreadings: The two claims get collapsed. Reports that implicit self-esteem measures have failed are read as saying that the letter preference itself is gone, when that preference is among the better-replicated findings in the area. The traffic runs the other way too, with the robustness of the letter preference offered as warrant for whatever the task is being used to measure. Buhrmester, Blanton and Swann draw the line: the task measures something, and that something looks like implicit egotism rather than self-worth. The effect is also not confined to initials, and Nuttin's own analyses separate first-name from family-name letters and initials from non-initials. Nor does it spread to letters standing for anything a person merely belongs to. Hoorens's review reports that Nuttin found no preference for national initials, F for a French rater, and none for the capital letters marking a car's country of origin. Johnson found none for the letters of a person's home town. The career and marriage claims built from the same premise belong to a separate literature and are covered under nominative determinism.
